overview: This atlas card wears a language label like a pretend crown. Its only polygon appears from 200 to 100 BCE, covering an irregular sweep from lower Myanmar through mainland Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. Yet “Mon-Khmer” is a later scholarly classification, not a recorded ancient self-name, kingdom, ethnicity, or border. Linguists now usually discuss Austroasiatic languages, and they still debate the family's internal branches and prehistoric dispersal. Archaeology gives a richer, messier picture. Named sites reveal rice farming, fishing, salt making, iron tools, copper production, beads, pottery, textiles, burials, travel, and growing exchange. Khao Sam Kaeo connected craftspeople across seas. Ban Non Wat and Noen U-Loke preserve changing communities on the Khorat Plateau. Go O Chua shows salt work, bone craft, burials, and possible music. Cambodian cemeteries reveal care, inequality, and sometimes violence. None proves which language every resident spoke. No securely localized writing from this century can be assigned to the polygon's supposed speakers, so there is no honest ancient text sample. The map layer disappears at 100 BCE, but people, settlements, languages, and regional networks continue. Think of the shape as a warning label, then meet the communities evidence can actually show.

periods.title: 200 to 190 BCE: one polygon, many communities
periods.summary: The exact feature appears only in the 200 BCE snapshot. Its huge shape is an editorial language-family guess, while excavated settlements, cemeteries and workshops document different regional histories that cannot be merged into one state or people.

periods.title: 190 to 180 BCE: rice landscapes differ
periods.summary: Plant remains show rice at mainland and peninsular sites, but field systems, gathering, fishing and imported crops varied. These ten-year slices organize evidence; archaeology cannot date a supposed family-wide change to this decade.

periods.title: 180 to 170 BCE: workshops connect distant skills
periods.summary: Khao Sam Kaeo preserves metal, glass and hard-stone production linked to several technological traditions. Mobile specialists and local learners made a cosmopolitan workshop community, not evidence that foreign visitors founded or ruled the whole region.

periods.title: 170 to 160 BCE: salt and river exchange matter
periods.summary: At Go O Chua, earlier salt-making debris and later burials show a long-lived lower Mekong place. Salt, bone tools, pottery and waterways connected households without revealing one language, government or fixed ethnic frontier.

periods.title: 160 to 150 BCE: burials preserve unequal memories
periods.summary: Cemeteries record children and adults, pots, tools, ornaments and changing funeral choices. Grave wealth can suggest distinction, but it does not provide a complete census, family tree or direct photograph of everyday rank.

periods.title: 150 to 140 BCE: metals travel through networks
periods.summary: Copper from central Laos and varied metalworking traditions entered wide exchange systems. Ores, ingots, objects and technical knowledge could travel by different routes, so a shared bronze or iron form does not prove shared speech or political control.

periods.title: 140 to 130 BCE: bodies reveal health and work
periods.summary: Teeth, bones and injuries offer evidence for diet, illness, labor and violence at particular cemeteries. They rarely identify a healer, remedy or language, and excavated samples represent only part of each living community.

periods.title: 130 to 120 BCE: coasts and interiors exchange differently
periods.summary: Peninsular ports, inland farming settlements, mining zones and lower Mekong communities participated in overlapping networks. Exchange brought goods and ideas, while local makers selected and transformed them rather than receiving one ready-made civilization package.

periods.title: 120 to 110 BCE: later kingdoms are still later
periods.summary: Funan, Dvaravati, historic Mon polities and the Khmer Empire belong to later centuries. Archaeologists study long continuities, but this polygon cannot turn future names into rulers, identities or successors for people living before 100 BCE.

periods.title: 110 to 100 BCE: the color vanishes, life continues
periods.summary: The target disappears at the 100 BCE seam without a documented conquest or collapse. Other atlas layers take over sampled places, while real settlements, exchange, languages and families continue along their own uneven timelines.

sections.title: Start with the map label, language problem, and missing writing

items.text: The index calls this record “Mon-Khmer,” dates it from 200 to 100 BCE, and imports it as a state. Coverage finds exactly one border file. Decoding all fifty atlas snapshots confirms one feature in 200 BCE and none before or after. That is a database identity, not proof of an ancient country.

The polygon stretches from about 94 to 109 degrees east and 1 to 19 degrees north. It owns sampled Bago, Bangkok, Khorat, Cambodia, the Mekong delta, Kedah and Kuala Lumpur, yet excludes Chiang Mai, the Red River and Sa Huynh. One shared arc with thai-bc200 exposes editorial partitioning.

“Mon-Khmer” was used for many Austroasiatic languages outside Munda, often giving the famous written languages Mon and Khmer too much classificatory weight. Current specialists disagree over deep internal branches. A family relationship among languages therefore cannot supply a single ancient name, capital, ruler, culture or border.

Homeland and dispersal models are hypotheses built from reconstructed vocabulary, language comparison, archaeology and sometimes genetics. Sidwell's riverine model is one proposal, while Blench stresses how difficult it is to align language families with crops or artifacts. The atlas turns debate into a certainty its sources do not support.

Written-language sample: none securely attested. No reviewed inscription from 200 to 100 BCE can be localized to this polygon and assigned to its supposed Austroasiatic speakers. The earliest regional inscriptions and named kingdoms belong to later centuries. A later Sanskrit, Mon, Khmer or Tamil text would be a misleading substitute.

sections.title: Travel through distinct Iron Age regions without blending them

items.text: On the Khorat Plateau, sites such as Ban Non Wat and Noen U-Loke preserve long sequences of settlement and burial. Archaeologists debate exact phase dates, and the Iron Age spans centuries. Evidence from one excavated square cannot stand for every village inside the atlas shape, much less for one language community.

Go O Chua in southern Vietnam combined settlement and cemetery evidence near the Vam Co Tay River. Its layers include pottery, bone and metal objects, salt-making debris and later burials. These materials name activities at a place; they do not label residents “Mon-Khmer” or reveal a province of an unknown state.

Khao Sam Kaeo on the upper Thai-Malay Peninsula was an unusually connected port and production center whose history began centuries before this card. Earthworks, craft areas and imported or transferred technologies show organized local action. Calling it merely an outpost erases the people who selected, learned and remade distant techniques.

Prohear in southeastern Cambodia preserves burials mainly from the late second century BCE into the first century CE, so only part of its cemetery may overlap this card. Gold, silver, bronze, pottery and beads reveal exchange and mortuary choices. The site's later excavated dates must not be pulled backward wholesale.

Sa Huynh jar-burial communities in central Vietnam followed their own archaeological trajectory and maritime connections. The exact polygon even excludes the Sa Huynh point sampled in this audit. Scholars debate later links to Cham history, but neither Sa Huynh nor Austronesian identity should be swallowed by an Austroasiatic-colored map.

sections.title: Build homes, fetch water, manage waste, and admit the toilet gap

items.text: Most houses used wood, bamboo, thatch, earth and other materials that decay in tropical soil. Postholes, hard floors, wall foundations and activity areas survive unevenly. Archaeologists reconstruct buildings from these traces, but a regional house form cannot identify its builders' language, and later houses cannot be copied backward unchanged.

Settlements often occupied mounds or raised ground near rivers and floodplains. Water supported drinking, cooking, washing, fishing, transport and crops while also bringing floods, mud and disease risk. Site location reveals practical choices, but it does not preserve who carried each jar or how household tasks were divided.

Some famous circular ditches and reservoirs around northeast Thai settlements belong mainly to later Iron Age phases. Direct dating warns against decorating every 200 BCE village with a perfect moat. Earlier residents still managed runoff, paths, fields and seasonal water, but the engineering visible today accumulated over long periods.

Floors, hearths, broken pots, animal bone, plant remains and craft waste mark household work. People surely swept, dumped refuse and kept useful areas passable, yet excavation rarely preserves a chore roster. A tidy floor can reflect repeated maintenance, erosion or later disturbance, so cleanliness should not be romanticized.

Toilet fact, with the glamour removed: no reviewed source securely identifies a standard latrine, sewer or waste-collection system for these communities in 200 to 100 BCE. People had to manage bodily waste and washing somehow, but the evidence does not justify drawing a cute bamboo toilet over a stream.

sections.title: Meet families, children, neighbors, and unequal social worlds

items.text: Cemeteries include women, men, infants and older children, sometimes clustered or arranged in rows. Those patterns may reflect households, kin, residence groups or ritual categories, but bones alone do not print a family tree. Missing children may reflect preservation or burial customs rather than indifference to them.

Children could receive pots, beads, bangles or special containers in some cemeteries. Such care makes young people visible, but grave goods do not tell us whether every child owned those objects in life. A wealthy infant burial can signal inherited standing, community ritual, grief, or several meanings together.

Burial goods sometimes differ by age, sex or cluster, yet they are poor job badges. A sickle beside a skeleton may carry economic, personal or ceremonial meaning. Researchers test patterns across many graves before proposing gendered labor, and responsible readers keep conclusions local rather than assigning chores to an entire language family.

Quantitative work shows social inequality changing through time at Ban Non Wat and neighboring sites. Rich and modest graves existed, while later phases followed different patterns. Burial wealth records funeral investment, not a bank statement. It can reveal distinction without proving kings, classes or hereditary rule in every settlement.

Isotopes can compare where people obtained food and whether individuals grew up locally, but even promising residence models remain hypotheses. One study asks whether prehistoric Thai communities were matrilocal rather than announcing the answer. Family arrangements probably varied by site, generation, marriage, mobility and circumstance.

sections.title: Learn at home and in workshops without inventing schools

items.text: No classroom, textbook or school register survives from this polygon's century. Children and newcomers probably learned by watching, helping, practicing and being corrected in households, fields, boats and workshops. That is an inference from skilled production sequences, not proof that every craft followed one formal apprenticeship system.

Metalworkers controlled heat, fuel, ores, crucibles, moulds and timing. At Khao Sam Kaeo, several technological traditions appear together, suggesting movement of knowledge and perhaps craftspeople. A learner could ruin a batch spectacularly; slag and broken technical ceramics are the archaeological leftovers of demanding experiments and routine production.

Glass workers shaped bracelets and beads by hot and cold techniques. Compositional study connects workshops across the upper peninsula while also finding local variation. Skills could travel with people, objects or demonstrations. Similar beads therefore show networks and choices, not automatic ethnic identity or an invisible foreign colony.

Farm knowledge included reading soils, rain, weeds, seed condition, pests and harvest timing. Plant remains show rice systems changing across sites and centuries. Children could learn useful tasks in small steps, but archaeobotany cannot tell us their starting age, whether instruction was kind, or who got the least popular jobs.

Potters learned clay selection, temper, forming, drying and firing; bead makers added grinding, drilling and polishing; bone workers planned around an animal's anatomy. Finished objects hide errors, while debris preserves practice. None of these technical traditions requires literacy, and no exact-period script sample can be assigned to the learners.

sections.title: Grow rice, catch fish, gather plants, and make salt

items.text: Rice mattered, but a rice grain cannot identify a language. At Khao Sam Kaeo, charred grains, husks and weeds indicate food use and cultivation practices; preservation favors some plant parts over others. Households also relied on resources that vanished, were never burned, or have not yet been sampled.

Khao Sam Kaeo and nearby exchange sites yielded rice alongside pulses and other plants arriving through regional networks. Imported crops did not create an imported population by themselves. Local cooks could accept a new bean, reject another ingredient, and fit unfamiliar plants into meals that left frustratingly few recognizable recipes.

Fish, shellfish, pigs, wild animals and gathered plants supplemented cultivated foods at many mainland sites. Bones and shells identify ingredients better than dishes. A pot containing fish remains might have held soup, processing waste or a ritual offering, so archaeologists avoid publishing a confident prehistoric menu from one messy vessel.

At Go O Chua, masses of ceramic supports called briquetage helped researchers reconstruct brine heating for salt. Archaeomagnetic analysis tested how the pieces sat during firing. Salt preserved and flavored food and could travel in exchange, but industrial debris does not reveal who controlled production or how workers were rewarded.

Food could mark inequality in funerals as well as meals. At Noen U-Loke, some later graves were lined with clay and filled with rice, yet that spectacular practice postdates much of this card. It shows why rice in a grave should not be counted as an ordinary dinner serving.

sections.title: Forge iron, cast copper, shape beads, pots, cloth, and bone

items.text: Iron sickles, knives, points and axes changed cutting, farming and conflict, but tools remained valuable work rather than magical upgrades. Smiths needed suitable ore or metal, charcoal, furnaces and repeated forging. The distribution of finished objects depended on repair, exchange and access, so not every household owned the same toolkit.

The Vilabouly Complex in central Laos preserves mining and primary copper production across Bronze and Iron Age phases. Lead-isotope and metallographic work links much of its metal to local sources and wider exchange. This is evidence for a production node, not a copper empire whose borders match the atlas polygon.

Researchers experimentally co-smelted malachite and chalcocite in crucibles to test how Vilabouly remains might have formed. The experiment produced products comparable to archaeological samples. It strengthens one technical explanation but does not prove each ancient firing followed the recipe or that modern experimenters recreated workers' beliefs and organization.

Glass and stone ornaments crossed long distances, while some workshops produced them locally. Chemical signatures, waste and half-finished pieces help separate manufacture from mere ownership. A bead at a grave can show adornment and connection; it cannot by itself identify the wearer's language, birthplace, religion or political loyalty.

Spindle whorls point to thread making, while fabrics usually rot. Pottery survives better and carries traces of forming, decoration, firing and use. Bone waste at Go O Chua reveals planned cutting and shaping. These quiet crafts required patience, including the ancient superpower of making many nearly matching things by hand.

sections.title: Face illness, injury, birth, care, and medical uncertainty

items.text: Skeletons can preserve cavities, infection, anemia indicators, arthritis, injuries and growth disruption. They rarely reveal every disease, and soft tissue is mostly gone. Bioarchaeologists compare age, sex, lesions and burial context, then state probabilities. A bone change is evidence for a bodily experience, not an ancient doctor's written diagnosis.

Dental studies at Cambodian Iron Age cemeteries compare cavities, tooth loss and wear, which can reflect food, age, biology and how teeth were used. Rice agriculture does not produce one automatic dental result. Different preparation methods, other foods and sampling all complicate the tempting story that one crop explains every mouth.

Healed fractures or long survival with injury can imply treatment, rest, food sharing and practical care, but they do not identify a medicine name. Unhealed trauma records danger without telling whether death followed immediately. Families and specialists probably used plant and ritual knowledge, yet no exact-period medical manual survives here.

Infant and maternal risk was serious, but cemeteries are not direct mortality registers. Later northeast Thai phases show many newborn burials and changing water landscapes; those findings cannot be pasted onto 200 BCE. Birth assistance, feeding and recovery happened in social settings that archaeology only partly illuminates.

No reviewed evidence supports one “Mon-Khmer medicine,” hospital system or universal remedy. Regional people had learned ways to clean wounds, support bodies, prepare foods and respond to pain, but effectiveness and access varied. Honest history credits care while refusing to prescribe an unevaluated ancient treatment to modern children.

sections.title: Remember the dead, wear ornaments, make music, and avoid one religion

items.text: Mainland communities buried some dead extended, flexed or in jars, with arrangements that changed by place and time. Pots, tools, food traces and ornaments may have helped mourners express memory, identity or obligation. Archaeologists can describe patterns, but the exact words, songs and hopes spoken at a grave are gone.

Prohear's graves included carefully placed ceramics, ornaments and implements, with some bodies wrapped in fiber mats. Precious metals show skilled alloying and wide exchange. Wealthy burial does not prove that the dead ruled a kingdom, and looting means the excavated sample preserves only part of the original cemetery.

At Go O Chua, researchers studied two shaped deer-antler objects as possible chordophones. Microscopic manufacture marks support careful craft, while the musical identification remains an interpretation because strings did not survive. Fun fact: an ancient instrument candidate can be both exciting and followed by a scholarly question mark.

Sa Huynh jar burials used varied jar forms and included iron objects and ornaments in some regions. Similar practices around seas suggest interaction, but jars did not carry passports. The tradition's origins and connections remain debated, and it must not be renamed “Mon-Khmer” simply because an atlas polygon approaches central Vietnam.

Later Brahmanic and Buddhist art, Indic-derived scripts, Mon inscriptions and Old Khmer texts belong to later historical settings. Early exchange with South Asia preceded their secure local appearance. This card therefore discusses ritual through burials and objects, without backdating named religions or borrowing a later inscription as a pretend contemporary voice.

sections.title: Confront conflict, celebrate achievements, and reject a fake ending

items.text: Weapons occur in graves and settlements, but an iron point can serve hunting, display or warfare. Context matters. At Phum Snay, unusually frequent head injuries and swords support interpersonal violence more strongly than weapons alone. Even there, the cemetery spans centuries and cannot make every household permanently warlike.

Ditches, banks, fields, workshops and cemeteries required coordinated labor. Coordination could arise through households, local leaders, reciprocal work, obligation or coercion, and evidence rarely selects one mechanism. Large construction shows collective capacity; it does not automatically reveal a king, bureaucracy or state matching the map color.

Ancient DNA reveals repeated mixture and movement across Southeast Asia. Genetic similarity does not equal language, ethnicity or political identity, and present communities are not fossils. Studies of ancient and modern genomes specifically show complexity among Austroasiatic-speaking populations, undermining a simple one-people migration painted across this polygon.

Achievements belonged to miners, smelters, farmers, fishers, salt workers, potters, weavers, bead makers, builders, healers, travelers, carers and mourners. Regional exchange joined their work without flattening it. The impressive story is a web of local experiments and connections, not one lost empire invented from a language-family label.

At 100 BCE the exact mon-khmer feature simply disappears. Its Bago and Thaton probes pass to arakan, many mainland and peninsula probes pass to thai-bc100, and eastern probes change differently. No reviewed source records a matching collapse, conquest or mass disappearance, so the endpoint is an atlas seam with continuity.

ending.text: The exact mon-khmer polygon disappears in the 100 BCE atlas snapshot, but no documented state or people fell at that date. The label was a modern linguistic shortcut placed over many archaeological regions for one century. Settlements, households, crafts, exchange networks and ancestral languages continued along different paths. Later Funan, Dvaravati, Mon polities and Khmer states have their own evidence and cannot be declared automatic successors. The honest ending is an editorial seam, not extinction, conquest or the birth of one new civilization.
